title: LemuroIDEA
text:
I remember a science activity when I was a child wherein I was tasked with finding a small insect or some such creature. Then I had a little decision tree with questions like “how many legs does it have?” to help me classify my critter. I remember it being really convenient in comparison to flipping through a giant book of insects, and I’ve often looked for a similar approach for quick classification, but without much luck. Which is probably an indication that my forth-grade science workbook was overly simplified.
Photo by Dmytro Koplyk on Unsplash

title: LemuroIDEA
text:
But . . . maybe?
But what if we tried it? Maybe not with insects, there’s just too many for a simple proof of concept. And it would also be nice to sidestep geography as a factor. Usually if you’re trying to figure out what an organism is, you’ll first want to know where it came from, but that’s not in the spirit of my childhood memory. And while we’re at it, let’s choose something charismatic.
I’m thinking lemurs. They’re a pretty unusual group of animals, with just over 100 species. They’re limited in range to the island of Madagascar, checking another box for our POC.
Plus, just look at ’em!



D’awww.


Photo by Molnár Tamás Photography™ on Unsplash

title: LemuroIDEA
text:
Getting the data
While wandering down a Wiki rabbit hole some years ago, I found the ITIS taxonomic database. I believe this will do for our purposes!

Data Attribution
The data used in this post is the Lemuroidea superfamily taxonomic dataset, sourced directly from the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS). This publicly available dataset provides automated taxonomic data on lemurs, including valid scientific ranks, statuses, and hierarchical classifications.
I downloaded a tsv of the Lemuroidea superfamily, and we can have a quick look at it:

library(readr)
library(dplyr)

lemurs <- read_tsv("lemur_taxa.txt")

colnames(lemurs)

 [9] "order"                    "superfamily"             
[11] "family"                   "genus"                   
[13] "subgenus"                 "specificEpithet"         
[15] "infraspecificEpithet"     "taxonRank"               
[17] "taxonomicStatus"          "modified"                
[19] "namePublishedIn"          "scientificNameID"        
[21] "verbatimTaxonRank"        "taxonRemarks"            
[23] "higherClassification"    


And let’s get them organized a little bit:

# Filter for valid species to build an accurate classification baseline
valid_species <- lemurs %>% 
  filter(taxonRank == "species", taxonomicStatus == "valid")

glimpse(valid_species)

# Calculate how many unique species exist within each Genus and Family branch
lemur_tree_branches <- valid_species %>%
  group_by(family, genus) %>%
  summarise(species_count = n_distinct(specificEpithet), .groups = "drop")

# Print the resulting breakdown as a readable reference table
print(lemur_tree_branches)

title: LemuroIDEA
text:
Making a tree

library(collapsibleTree)

collapsibleTree(
  valid_species,
  hierarchy = c("family", "genus", "specificEpithet"),
  root = "Lemuroidea",
  zoomable = TRUE,
  collapsed = TRUE
)







Figure 1: Interactive taxonomic tree of the Lemuroidea superfamily from Family down to individual Species.




And that’s pretty fun! I don’t have little questions to help navigate, but I’ll come back to this. Someday.

title: Ariana Montgomery
text: Hi! I’m Ariana, a Master of Data Science student at the University of British Columbia. After graduating with a couple of bachelor’s degrees, I worked as full-stack developer for a few years, then as a data engineer of various stripes for another 15. I’m here to formalize and expand my knowledge of the field.

title: About
text:
I attended Harding University in Searcy, Arkansas for my undergraduate. I wound up with two degrees: a BS in Mathematics and Computer Science and a BA in Spanish. I was magna cum laude and a graduate from the Honors College with distinction.
I worked as a full-stack .NET developer for a couple of years, and then I found data! In the last 15 years I’ve done everything from DBA tasks to client-facing reporting suites. I’ve had a variety of titles and responsibilities, but data has been at the center of them all.

title: About
text:
Area of Focus
Because of my time in sundry operations roles, I’m particularly interested in building QA systems that detect issues in both input and output. Ideally these systems not only provide early warning of invalid input (such as nulls or duplicates) and drift (like an anomalously small or large amount of input), but also do so in an automated, ongoing manner that ensures the output is correct over the system’s whole lifecycle.

title: About
text:
Reading
Outside of work, I love to read. I have a spreadsheet of every book I’ve read for the last ten years, and I will happily and endlessly chat about it. Horror, science fiction, and fantasy are my favorite genres, but I’ve been known to pick up just about anything. I’m also always looking for recommendations, so tell me about your favorite books, too!

title: Let Me Explain
text: You may have noticed a couple of unusual choices on this site. So right off the bat, please let me explain . . .

title: Let Me Explain
text:
My Profile Picture
As a wedding present to me, my husband (cool guy, I like him a lot) commissioned a drawing from an artist friend of ours. I used the close-up of my face as a placeholder some years ago and never got around to getting a replacement. The full drawing looks like this:



Slaughtering zombies with lightsabers from the back of a velociraptor


Said artist friend winces whenever he looks at it and says he can do better. But I’m inordinately fond of it and don’t care if he “learned a lot in art school” or if his “style has matured” since then.

title: Let Me Explain
text:
My GitHub Username
My way of being a rebellious teenager was to listen exclusively to classical opera music. (Yes, I was an exceedingly odd child.) I still very much enjoy it, but no longer consider myself much of a nerd about the topic. Nevertheless, the username has stuck around, and it’s never bothered me enough to change it.
